newsitem.title: USA: Lawmaker accuses U.S. Treasury of stalling tactics.
newsitem.headline: Lawmaker accuses U.S. Treasury of stalling tactics.

text.p: A lawmaker has charged the Treasury Department with using stalling tactics to avoid answering questions about how community development grants were awarded.

Spencer Bachus, chairman of the House banking subcommittee on oversight, said a Treasury decision to refer questions about funding from the Community Development Financial Institutions (CDFI) grant program to Treasury's Office of the Inspector General was "simply unacceptable."
Published reports have linked some CDFI grants to firms in Arkansas that Bachus said had "well-documented ties to President and Mrs Clinton."
But a senior Treasury official said the decision to refer the matter to the Inspector General was simply a "prudent" effort to try to avoid having it treated as a partisan issue.
"The Inspector-General's work is designed to avoid politics," the Treasury official said, "We're trying to keep politics out of this."

In a letter sent to Treasury Secretary Robert Rubin on Wednesday, Bachus said Treasury files "do not provide a clear explanation of how particular applicants were selected over others" and called for an accounting of how taxpayers' funds were used.

Bachus said the referral to the Inspector General was "an outright political stall" designed to avoid answering questions before his subcommittee. It could take many months for the Inspector General to investigate, he noted.
CDFI was set up to foster the growth of community development banks that make small loans to businesspeople in poorer areas of the country.

In a news release, Bachus said that out of 264 applications for CDFI grants in the first round, "five institutions with well-documented ties to President and Mrs Clinton were selected to receive over one-third of the grant money."
But the senior Treasury official said Bachus' charge was "a little over-the-top, adding: "There's no evidence of that."

Treasury insists all CDFI funds selections were "based on merit" but said the fund was strengthening its internal controls and processes and Treasury planned to hire more people to oversee and administer the program.
